set1.q: Iron accumulation in the pituitary in hemochromatosis can lead to which disorder?
opts: Correct. Iron accumulation can affect the pituitary and lead to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism: decreased libido, impotence or amenorrhea, with small testicular size, gynecomastia and reduced body hair on examination.
The lesion described is in the pituitary, so the gonads fail for lack of stimulation rather than from a primary testicular defect. Tell: the term is hypogonadotropic, a low-signal problem from above.
Cardiomyopathy is a cardiac manifestation of hemochromatosis, from iron deposited in the heart. Tell: the pituitary clinical pearl is about libido, impotence and amenorrhea.
Skin bronzing of the face, neck, groin and extensor surfaces is iron in the skin. Tell: pituitary iron causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

set1.q: What level of fetal hemoglobin seems to be the threshold for decreased clinical severity of sickle cell disease or beta thalassemia?
opts: Less than 1 percent is the normal abundance of fetal hemoglobin in adults, far below the protective threshold. Tell: protection needs the 10 to 20 percent seen in hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin.
A few percent is still far below the protective level; HbF has to reach about 10 to 20 percent to lessen severity. Tell: the threshold is a two-digit percentage.

Correct. Fetal hemoglobin is normally less than 1 percent. In hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin, expression is variable, but 10 to 20 percent HbF seems to be the threshold for decreased severity of sickle cell disease or beta thalassemia.
60 to 70 percent is the glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency prevalence among Kurdish Jews, not a fetal hemoglobin level. Tell: the HbF threshold is 10 to 20 percent.

set1.q: When is referral to hematology recommended in iron deficiency anemia?
opts: Any gastrointestinal bleed found on workup

A gastrointestinal bleed calls for a gastrointestinal consult for colonoscopy or endoscopy to evaluate for colorectal cancer, not a hematology referral. Tell: the bleed goes to the gut specialist; an unexplained or unresponsive anemia goes to hematology.
Heavy menstrual loss as the identified cause

Menstrual blood loss is treated directly, with an oral contraceptive (consider continuous-cycle) and iron replacement. Tell: a known, treatable cause does not need hematology; failure of oral iron or an unconfirmed diagnosis does.
Constipation that limits oral iron adherence
Constipation from ferrous sulfate is managed with a laxative or stool softener, and true intolerance leads to parenteral iron. Tell: side effects change the route, not the specialist.
No response to oral iron or unclear diagnosis

Correct. Referral to hematology is recommended if the diagnosis is not confirmed or the patient is unresponsive to oral iron therapy. Otherwise treatment means treating the underlying cause and replacing iron.

set1.q: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia carries an increased risk of which complication?
opts: All hemolytic anemias retain the products of red cell destruction, including iron, but iron overload is not the complication flagged as an important note for autoimmune hemolysis. Tell: that complication is a clot, venous thromboembolism.
Acute chest syndrome is the leading cause of death in sickle cell disease, not a complication of antibody-mediated hemolysis. Tell: autoimmune hemolysis raises the risk of venous clots.
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism follows iron accumulating in the pituitary in hemochromatosis. Tell: autoimmune hemolysis carries a thrombotic risk, deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.

Correct. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is associated with an increased risk of venous thromboembolism, so consider a D-dimer and bilateral leg ultrasound for deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, give prophylaxis to inpatients and consider it in outpatients.

set1.q: What is the defining diagnostic feature of sideroblastic anemia?
opts: Basophilic stippling, an abnormal collection of nucleic acids in the cells, is the smear finding of lead poisoning. Tell: the sideroblastic hallmark is a ring of iron-filled mitochondria around the nucleus, seen in the marrow.

A dimorphic smear, with microcytic, normal and macrocytic cells, does occur in sideroblastic anemia but is not the defining feature. Tell: only the marrow aspirate shows the ring sideroblasts that define it.
Increased ferritin, serum iron and transferrin saturation reflect the excess total body iron, but ferritin also rises with inflammation. Tell: a lab value supports it; ring sideroblasts define it.

Correct. A bone marrow aspirate showing ring sideroblasts is the defining feature: iron-containing mitochondria form a basophilic ring around the nucleus. The blood shows variable microcytosis and hypochromia, a dimorphic smear and excess body iron.

set1.q: Below which hemoglobin is erythropoietin supplementation an approved indication in anemia of chronic disease?
opts: Waiting for a hemoglobin below 7 g/dL sets the bar too low; the approved threshold is less than 10 g/dL. Tell: the erythropoietin cut-off is 10.
A hemoglobin below 8 g/dL is lower than needed; erythropoietin is approved once it falls below 10 g/dL. Tell: the indication starts at 10, not 8.

Correct. Erythropoietin supplementation (epoetin alfa) is indicated for a hemoglobin less than 10 g/dL, in anemia due to rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, hepatitis C, zidovudine therapy in human immunodeficiency virus infection, myelosuppressive chemotherapy of a solid malignancy, or chronic kidney disease.
A threshold of 12 g/dL would treat milder anemia than the indication covers; the approved cut-off is less than 10 g/dL. Tell: 10 is the line.

set1.q: Why can a normal or elevated serum ferritin fail to exclude iron deficiency anemia?
opts: Ferritin reflects the serum iron level

Ferritin reflects iron stores and rises with inflammation; serum iron is a separate part of the iron panel. Tell: the trap is inflammation pushing ferritin up, not ferritin standing in for serum iron.

Microcytosis, a mean corpuscular volume below 80 fL, does not raise ferritin; in iron deficiency ferritin is reduced. Tell: what can falsely raise ferritin is an inflammatory condition, because ferritin is an acute phase reactant.

Reduced serum ferritin is part of the iron deficiency panel; the reason a normal value can mislead is inflammation, not a late fall. Tell: look for infection or autoimmune disease when ferritin looks reassuring.
Ferritin is an acute phase reactant

Correct. Ferritin and, to a lesser degree, transferrin are acute phase reactants, so a patient with an inflammatory condition (infection, autoimmune disease) who is also iron deficient may have a normal or even elevated ferritin. A normal or elevated ferritin does not exclude iron deficiency anemia.

set1.q: Pernicious anemia raises the risk of which cancer?
opts: Correct. Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune reaction against parietal cells and/or intrinsic factor, which results in atrophy of the gastric mucosa and an increased risk of gastric cancer. A gastric biopsy may show chronic atrophic gastritis.

Colon cancer is not the malignancy tied to pernicious anemia; the autoimmune damage is in the stomach. Tell: the risk follows the organ under attack, the parietal cells of the gastric mucosa, so the cancer is gastric.

Acute myeloid leukemia is a clonal abnormality that can develop in aplastic anemia, with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and myelodysplastic syndrome. Tell: clonal marrow disorders follow aplastic anemia; gastric cancer follows pernicious anemia.

Myelodysplastic syndrome is linked to acquired sideroblastic anemia and is a clonal abnormality after aplastic anemia. Tell: pernicious anemia causes gastric atrophy, and its cancer risk is gastric cancer.

set1.q: Which antibiotic is associated with aplastic anemia?
opts: Isoniazid is a drug cause of acquired, reversible sideroblastic anemia, with chlorambucil, alcohol, copper deficiency and lead. Tell: isoniazid points to ring sideroblasts; chloramphenicol points to stem cell loss and pancytopenia.
Phenytoin is listed as a cause of folate deficiency, giving a macrocytic megaloblastic anemia. Tell: phenytoin depletes folate; the antibiotic on the aplastic anemia list is chloramphenicol.
Metformin is a drug cause of folate deficiency, not of aplastic anemia, and it is not an antibiotic. Tell: the aplastic anemia drug list names chloramphenicol and cytotoxic agents.

Correct. Chloramphenicol is a drug associated with aplastic anemia, with cytotoxic or chemotherapeutic agents, ionizing radiation and toxins such as benzene and pesticides. Direct injury to hematopoietic stem cells is one of its pathophysiologic processes.

set1.q: How is glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency inherited, and who is generally affected?
opts: Nothing about this enzyme deficiency is autosomal; it is X-linked recessive. Tell: a male patient and an unaffected carrier mother is the classic pattern of an X-linked recessive disorder.

Correct. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is X-linked recessive, so generally males are affected. Carrier females have two populations of red cells, one normal and one deficient, and are generally unaffected.

Autosomal recessive inheritance belongs to primary hemochromatosis, a disorder of the genes that control iron absorption. Tell: the enzyme deficiency rides on the X chromosome, which is why males carry the burden.
Carrier females have two populations of red cells, one normal and one deficient, and are generally unaffected. Tell: the inheritance is recessive and the affected patient is usually male.

set1.q: How many alpha and beta globin genes does a person normally carry?
opts: Four alpha genes is right, but there are only two beta globin genes. Tell: count the alpha notation, aa/aa, for four, and remember beta is half that.

Correct. There are 4 alpha globin genes and 2 beta globin genes, and the thalassemia phenotype depends on how many are mutated: from a silent carrier with one alpha gene affected (a-/aa) to a form incompatible with life.
This reverses the counts: alpha globin has four genes, beta globin two. Tell: the silent carrier notation a-/aa shows four alpha slots, two on each chromosome.
Two beta genes is right, but alpha globin has four genes, two on each chromosome. Tell: the alpha trait notations aa/-- and a-/a- each show four alpha positions.

set1.q: Which drug is the disease-modifying therapy that raises fetal hemoglobin in sickle cell disease?
opts: Rituximab is a treatment option for autoimmune hemolytic anemia, after glucocorticoids. Tell: sickle cell disease is not antibody mediated, and its disease-modifying drug is hydroxyurea.

Correct. Disease modification in sickle cell disease is hydroxyurea, which raises fetal hemoglobin (HbF) and reduces vaso-occlusive events. Prevention adds vaccinations, childhood penicillin prophylaxis and infection education.
Penicillin prophylaxis is childhood prevention against infection, not disease modification. Tell: the drug that changes the disease itself does so by raising HbF.
Folic acid is on the supportive treatment list for thalassemia and does not raise fetal hemoglobin. Tell: the disease-modifying drug for sickle cell disease is hydroxyurea.

set1.q: Which bilirubin pattern is expected in hemolytic anemia?
opts: Both fractions are likely elevated, and the unconjugated fraction is the larger one, since it is what macrophages release. Tell: an isolated conjugated rise does not match red cell breakdown upstream of the liver.

Correct. Both bilirubin fractions are likely elevated in hemolytic anemia, with unconjugated greater than conjugated. Macrophages break down red cells and release unconjugated bilirubin, which the liver then conjugates, so the unconjugated fraction leads.

This reverses the pattern: the bilirubin released by macrophages destroying red cells is unconjugated and is only conjugated afterward in the liver. Tell: hemolysis floods the system upstream of the liver, so unconjugated leads.

Hemolysis releases hemoglobin whose breakdown raises bilirubin, and clinical jaundice appears once the total exceeds 2.0 mg/dL. Tell: bilirubin is one of the three tests added to the hemolysis algorithm because it rises.

set1.q: What is the treatment of primary hemochromatosis?
opts: Transfusion adds iron and can exacerbate overload, as it does in thalassemia. Tell: the overloaded patient needs iron removed by phlebotomy.
Glucocorticoids are the initial treatment of autoimmune hemolytic anemia, not a way to remove iron. Tell: primary hemochromatosis is treated by removing iron with therapeutic phlebotomy.

Correct. Primary hemochromatosis is treated with therapeutic phlebotomy with ferritin-guided follow-up. Secondary overload is managed by treating the cause, with chelation considered when phlebotomy is unsuitable.
Chelation is considered for secondary overload when phlebotomy is unsuitable, not as the first treatment of primary disease. Tell: primary disease is treated by removing blood.

set1.q: Which medication class is singled out as a cause of iron deficiency anemia?
opts: Isoniazid, an antituberculosis drug, is a reversible cause of sideroblastic anemia, not of iron deficiency. Tell: isoniazid points to ring sideroblasts; acid suppression points to iron deficiency.

Folate antagonists such as methotrexate are linked to folate deficiency and a macrocytic anemia, not to iron deficiency. Tell: a large-cell anemia suggests a folate problem, while proton pump inhibitors go with a small-cell iron deficiency.

Loop diuretics are not named among the causes of iron deficiency, which are blood loss, dietary factors and medications such as antacids and proton pump inhibitors, malabsorption and increased demand. Tell: the drug named is an acid suppressant.

Correct. Among the dietary factors behind iron deficiency, antacids (calcium) and medications, particularly proton pump inhibitors, are listed. A patient on long-term acid suppression with a microcytic anemia should have that medication reviewed.

set1.q: Which medication is listed as a cause of folate deficiency?
opts: Chloramphenicol is a drug associated with aplastic anemia, the loss of hematopoietic stem cells that causes pancytopenia. Tell: chloramphenicol empties the marrow; phenytoin depletes folate.

Proton pump inhibitors are a medication cause of iron deficiency anemia, which is microcytic. Tell: acid suppression is listed under iron deficiency; the folate drug list is methotrexate, 5-fluorouracil, hydroxyurea, phenytoin and metformin.

Correct. Phenytoin is on the list of drugs that cause folate deficiency, with methotrexate, 5-fluorouracil, hydroxyurea and metformin. A patient taking one of these with a macrocytic anemia should have folate deficiency considered.

Isoniazid is a drug cause of acquired, reversible sideroblastic anemia, with chlorambucil, alcohol, copper deficiency and lead poisoning. Tell: isoniazid belongs to the sideroblastic anemia list, not the folate drug list, where phenytoin is named.

set1.q: For an adolescent with heavy menses, which care priority is listed?
opts: Family screening for hemochromatosis is the adult row, since the gene-related disease usually presents in adults. Tell: in adolescents the listed concern is iron deficiency from heavy menses.
Correct. For adolescents with heavy menses, check a complete blood count and ferritin, treat iron deficiency and control the bleeding, while supporting adherence and the transition to adult care.
Neonatal complete blood count ranges are the infant priority, along with recognizing inherited anemias and abnormal newborn screens. Tell: the adolescent priority is heavy menses and iron deficiency.
Marrow disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome are on the elderly checklist, with drugs and chronic kidney disease. Tell: the adolescent row is about heavy menses, counts and ferritin.

set1.q: When are chelating agents used in lead poisoning?
opts: Correct. Treatment of lead poisoning starts by stopping exposure and is based on the lead level; in severe cases with neurologic effects, chelating agents can be used: succimer, dimercaprol or ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid. The neurologic system is the most vulnerable.
Treatment is based on the lead level, so a detectable level alone does not call for chelation. Tell: chelation is kept for severe cases with neurologic effects; exposure removal comes first.
Stopping the exposure is the first step in every case; chelation does not replace it. Tell: remove the source first, then chelate if severe with neurologic effects.
A microcytic, hypochromic anemia is a feature of lead poisoning but not by itself an indication for chelation. Tell: the trigger is severity with neurologic involvement.

set1.q: Which drug is listed as a reversible cause of sideroblastic anemia?
opts: Omeprazole is not a listed cause of sideroblastic anemia; the drugs named for the acquired, reversible type are isoniazid and chlorambucil. Tell: of these four drugs, only isoniazid is on that list.
Methotrexate is associated with folate deficiency and a macrocytic anemia rather than with sideroblastic anemia. Tell: the antituberculosis drug isoniazid is the sideroblastic culprit.

Epoetin alfa is erythropoietin supplementation for anemia of chronic disease, and sideroblastic anemia typically responds poorly to it; it is not a cause. Tell: it treats anemia, it does not produce ring sideroblasts.

Correct. The acquired, reversible type of sideroblastic anemia follows alcohol, certain drugs (isoniazid, chlorambucil), copper deficiency, hypothermia and lead poisoning. Removing the offending agent is the first treatment.

set1.q: Which features help differentiate a hemolytic anemia from the typical symptoms of anemia?
opts: Shortness of breath is a typical anemia symptom common to anemia in general. Tell: the clue that points to hemolysis is the breakdown product, such as jaundice or hematuria.
Spoon-shaped nails are not among the listed differentiating features of hemolysis. Tell: hemolysis shows up as jaundice, splenomegaly, joint pain and hematuria instead.

Correct. Typical anemia symptoms are fatigue, shortness of breath, chest pain and pallor. The differentiating features of hemolysis are jaundice, splenomegaly, joint pain and hematuria, which reflect red cell breakdown products and splenic destruction.

Fatigue and pallor belong to the typical symptoms of anemia in general, so they cannot separate hemolysis from other causes. Tell: the differentiating list adds jaundice, splenomegaly, joint pain and hematuria.

set1.q: After exposure to an oxidant drug, about how long is the usual lag before hemolysis appears in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency?
opts: Minutes is far too fast; drug-induced hemolysis has a lag of 2 to 3 days between the oxidant and the hemolysis. Tell: think of a patient who started an antibiotic a couple of days before the dark urine.
Hours is still too short; drug-induced hemolysis generally follows the exposure by 2 to 3 days. Tell: the timeline is days, which is why the drug history must reach back a few days.

Correct. Patients have no symptoms until exposed to oxidative stress. Drug-induced hemolysis is acute and of variable severity, generally with a lag of 2 to 3 days, and then brings abdominal pain, jaundice, dark urine and splenomegaly.
About 8 weeks is the timing of the confirmatory enzyme level after an attack, not the lag before hemolysis. Tell: the lag before symptoms is 2 to 3 days; the confirmatory test waits weeks.

set1.q: Conversion of which compound requires both B12 and folate?
opts: Methylmalonic acid builds up when L-methylmalonyl CoA is not converted to succinyl CoA, a step that requires only B12. Tell: the methylmalonic acid step is B12-only, which is why it separates B12 from folate deficiency.

Transferrin carries iron, and its saturation is part of the microcytic anemia workup with serum iron, total iron-binding capacity and ferritin. Tell: transferrin belongs to the iron panel, not to the B12 and folate pathway.

Transcobalamin is the protein absorbed B12 binds in the circulation before storage in the liver; it is a carrier, not a compound converted by both vitamins. Tell: the step needing B12 and folate together turns homocysteine into methionine.
Correct. Metabolism of homocysteine to methionine requires both B12 and folate. It is ordered with methylmalonic acid when B12 and folate levels are borderline or clinical suspicion continues.

set1.q: Under which condition does hemoglobin S polymerize and form the sickle shape?
opts: Correct. Sickle cell anemia comes from a mutation of a beta globin gene; hemoglobin S is two alpha globins and two mutant beta globins. Under conditions of low oxygen tension HbS can polymerize and form a sickle shape.
This reverses the trigger; HbS polymerizes when oxygen tension is low. Tell: the polymer forms where the hemoglobin has given up its oxygen.
Oxidant drugs cause hemolysis in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency by forming Heinz bodies. Tell: sickling is a physical polymerization of HbS at low oxygen tension.
Antibody coating of the red cell is autoimmune hemolytic anemia, detected by the Coombs test. Tell: sickling is intrinsic to the abnormal hemoglobin and is triggered by low oxygen.

set1.q: Which sign of iron deficiency anemia is the urge to eat things that are not food?
opts: Correct. Pica, the urge to eat things that are not food, is listed as common in iron deficiency anemia. It sits with fatigue, pallor, exertional shortness of breath, smooth tongue and the starred nail bed changes, cheilosis and Plummer-Vinson syndrome.
Cheilosis is a starred sign of iron deficiency, but it affects the corners of the lips rather than describing a craving. Tell: a craving is pica; a lip finding is cheilosis.
Koilonychia is the spoon-shaped, concave nail of iron deficiency, a physical nail finding, not an eating behavior. Tell: nails mean koilonychia, cravings mean pica.

Plummer-Vinson syndrome is a starred iron deficiency finding involving swallowing, not an urge to eat non-food items. Tell: a behavior of eating non-food things is pica; a swallowing problem is Plummer-Vinson syndrome.

set1.q: Which absolute neutrophil count range defines moderate neutropenia?
opts: An absolute neutrophil count below 500 cells per microliter is severe neutropenia, and with fever it is an emergency. Tell: moderate sits just above it, 500-999.

Correct. Neutropenia is graded by the absolute neutrophil count: mild 1,000-1,500, moderate 500-999 and severe below 500 cells per microliter. Severity, duration and immune status predict infection risk.
An absolute neutrophil count of 1,000-1,500 cells per microliter is mild neutropenia. Tell: moderate is the band below mild and above severe, 500-999.
The neutropenia grades stop at 1,500 cells per microliter, the top of the mild range, so this range lies above them. Tell: the three grades are below 500, 500-999 and 1,000-1,500.

set1.q: In anemia of chronic kidney disease, what does a low transferrin saturation with a normal or high ferritin indicate?
opts: Correct. A low transferrin saturation may indicate iron-restricted erythropoiesis despite a normal or high ferritin, because inflammation and hepcidin restrict the iron available to the marrow. The treatment step is to correct the iron deficiency.

A normal or high ferritin can look reassuring, but the low transferrin saturation shows the marrow is not getting enough iron. Tell: in chronic kidney disease the saturation, not the ferritin, decides whether iron is restricted.
A low transferrin saturation signals a restricted iron supply to the marrow, not excess iron. Tell: a low saturation is the opposite signal, iron that is stored or locked away but not available.

Folate deficiency causes a macrocytic megaloblastic anemia and is judged by folate and homocysteine levels, not by the iron panel. Tell: transferrin saturation and ferritin are iron tests; their mismatch means iron-restricted erythropoiesis.

set1.q: What does a serum ferritin below 30 ng/mL indicate in a patient with anemia of chronic disease?
opts: Serum ferritin values should be normal or increased in anemia of chronic disease, so a value below 30 ng/mL is not a falsely low inflammatory reading. Tell: a low ferritin despite inflammation is a real signal of iron deficiency.

Correct. In anemia of chronic disease serum ferritin should be normal or increased; a value below 30 ng/mL indicates coexistent iron deficiency. The labs are the same as for iron deficiency, with an erythrocyte sedimentation rate and/or C-reactive protein if inflammation is not apparent.

The expected pattern in chronic disease is a normal or increased ferritin, so a value under 30 ng/mL is not the usual finding. Tell: a low ferritin on top of inflammation means iron deficiency is present too.
Sideroblastic anemia shows excess total body iron with increased serum iron, transferrin saturation and ferritin, the opposite of a low ferritin. Tell: ring sideroblasts come with high ferritin.

set1.q: What is the trade-off of taking ferrous sulfate with food?
opts: Food reduces, not increases, the gastrointestinal side effects of ferrous sulfate, though it does reduce absorption. Tell: food is gentler on the stomach and weaker on uptake.

Correct. Taking ferrous sulfate with food reduces its side effects but also decreases absorption. The better-absorbed approach is on an empty stomach in the morning with a full glass of orange juice, whose low pH, citric acid and vitamin C aid uptake.
Food does not increase absorption or side effects; it lowers both. Tell: food buys comfort at the cost of uptake.
If food improved both comfort and absorption there would be no trade-off; food actually decreases absorption. Tell: the absorption-friendly option is an empty stomach with orange juice.

set1.q: What is the listed prognosis of megaloblastic anemia once treated?
opts: Delayed B12 care may leave deficits
Correct. With B12 or folate deficiency treated, counts improve, but delayed B12 treatment may leave neurologic deficits, which is why neurologic recovery is monitored during follow-up.

Prognosis that depends on severity and response to treatment is the aplastic anemia row. Tell: megaloblastic counts improve with treatment, and the risk is lasting neurologic deficit if B12 came late.
Persisting while the underlying disease is active describes anemia of chronic disease. Tell: megaloblastic anemia corrects with B12 or folate, apart from possible neurologic deficits.
Megaloblastic anemia is treated by correcting the B12 or folate deficiency, and counts improve. Tell: counts improve, and the warning is about deficits after delayed B12 treatment.

set1.q: What is the normal range for the mean corpuscular volume, the average size of red blood cells?
opts: The numbers 32-36 belong to the mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration, in grams per deciliter, the hemoglobin relative to cell size. Tell: cell volume is counted in femtoliters and runs 80-100, while 32-36 g/dL is a concentration.

A mean corpuscular volume of 60-80 fL is already microcytic, because microcytosis is defined as a value below 80 fL, the finding of iron deficiency anemia. Tell: the normal band starts where microcytosis ends, at 80 fL.

Correct. The mean corpuscular volume, the average size of the red blood cells, runs 80-100 femtoliters. Below 80 fL is microcytosis, the pattern of iron deficiency; above 100 fL is macrocytosis. Reading it is one of the first steps in sorting an anemia.
A mean corpuscular volume above 100 fL is macrocytosis, the pattern of a macrocytic anemia, not a normal cell size. Tell: the normal band ends at 100 fL, so anything above it is large-cell.

set2.q: Which haptoglobin result is expected with intravascular hemolysis?
opts: Jaundice tracks the bilirubin, which rises in hemolysis and becomes visible above 2.0 mg/dL; haptoglobin moves the other way. Tell: bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase go up, haptoglobin goes down.

Correct. In intravascular hemolysis, free hemoglobin released into the plasma is picked up by haptoglobin, which carries it to the liver, so haptoglobin is used up and becomes decreased or absent. The binding is not complete, which is why some hemoglobin also reaches the urine.
Haptoglobin is consumed, not produced in excess, when it binds the free hemoglobin of intravascular hemolysis. Tell: a value that rises with lysis is lactate dehydrogenase; haptoglobin falls.

A normal haptoglobin would mean no free hemoglobin is being cleared, which is the opposite of intravascular red cell destruction. Tell: haptoglobin is one of the three added hemolysis tests precisely because it drops.

set2.q: Which oral vitamin occasionally produces a response in sideroblastic anemia?
opts: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) replaces a B12 deficiency in megaloblastic anemia, not sideroblastic anemia. Tell: a dimorphic smear with ring sideroblasts points to pyridoxine, not B12.

Correct. There are occasional responses to oral pyridoxine in sideroblastic anemia. Treatment otherwise removes the offending agent if acquired, uses red cell transfusion when severe, and refers to hematology for diagnostic or transfusion support; recombinant erythropoietin typically does not help.
Folic acid corrects folate deficiency, a cause of macrocytic anemia, and is not the vitamin with occasional responses in sideroblastic anemia. Tell: the sideroblastic vitamin is pyridoxine.
Vitamin C is not a listed treatment for sideroblastic anemia, which already carries an excess of total body iron. Tell: pyridoxine is the sideroblastic option.

set2.q: How does the course of sickle-hemoglobin C disease compare with sickle cell anemia and sickle cell trait?
opts: Hemoglobin C does not polymerize like a second S would, so sickle-hemoglobin C disease is not identical to sickle cell anemia. Tell: its course falls between the anemia and the trait.

Correct. Hemoglobin C comes from a different beta globin mutation and does not polymerize. Sickle-hemoglobin C disease, the combination of one C and one S, generally has a course between sickle cell anemia and sickle cell trait.
Hemoglobin C does not polymerize, so pairing it with S gives a milder course than two S genes. Tell: sickle-hemoglobin C disease sits between sickle cell anemia and the trait.

Sickle-hemoglobin C disease generally has a course between sickle cell anemia and sickle cell trait, so it is not milder than the trait. Tell: its course falls between the trait and full sickle cell anemia.

set2.q: What is the most common cause of iron deficiency anemia in adults?
opts: Dietary factors such as a vegan diet or heavy tea drinking can cause iron deficiency, but they are not the leading cause in adults. Tell: in an adult with iron deficiency, look first for chronic blood loss from the gut or menses.

Malabsorption, after gastric bypass surgery or with celiac sprue or food allergies, is a recognized but less common cause. Tell: malabsorption is a second-line explanation once chronic gastrointestinal or menstrual blood loss is looked for.

Increased demand in pregnancy, or growth in infancy and adolescence, causes iron deficiency in those groups, but it is not the most common adult cause overall. Tell: demand explains a pregnant patient or a growing child; blood loss explains most adults.

Correct. Chronic blood loss, from the gastrointestinal tract or from menses, is the most common cause of iron deficiency anemia in adults. That is why treatment starts with finding and treating the source, such as a gastrointestinal bleed or heavy menstrual loss.

set2.q: Which population has the highest listed prevalence of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency?
opts: Nigerians are listed at 22 percent, high but well below the top of the list. Tell: the highest figure, 60 to 70 percent, belongs to Kurdish Jews.
Japanese and Korean people sit at the bottom of the list at 0 to 1 percent. Tell: this is the reverse end of the table; Kurdish Jews lead at 60 to 70 percent.
Thai people are listed at 17 percent. Tell: that sits in the middle of the table, far below the 60 to 70 percent of Kurdish Jews.

Correct. The prevalence list is led by Kurdish Jews at 60 to 70 percent, followed by Sardinians (4 to 35 percent by village), Nigerians (22 percent), Thai people (17 percent) and American Black people (11 to 12 percent).

set2.q: Macrocytic anemia is defined by a mean corpuscular volume above which value?
opts: 80 fL is the bottom of the normal mean corpuscular volume range (80-100 fL), so a value just above it is normal, not macrocytic. Tell: macrocytosis starts above the top of the normal range, 100 fL.

Correct. Macrocytic anemia is anemia with a mean corpuscular volume greater than 100 fL. The normal mean corpuscular volume is 80-100 fL, so anything above the top of that range is macrocytic, and the causes then split into megaloblastic and non-megaloblastic groups.

115 fL is the value non-megaloblastic causes usually stay below, so it helps split the causes rather than define macrocytosis. Tell: the definition is above 100 fL; the 115 fL line sorts megaloblastic from non-megaloblastic.
125 fL is far above the defining line; a cell this large is macrocytic, but it does not mark where macrocytosis begins. Tell: any mean corpuscular volume over 100 fL already counts as macrocytic.

set2.q: When is parenteral iron indicated for iron deficiency anemia?
opts: At diagnosis, before any oral iron trial

Parenteral iron is not the first route; it is indicated for patients who are intolerant of or refractory to oral preparations. Tell: oral iron comes first, and the parenteral route follows its intolerance or failure.
As first-line therapy for menstrual loss
Menstrual blood loss is not by itself a reason for parenteral iron; iron is replaced orally first. Tell: parenteral iron is chosen for oral intolerance or failure, not for the cause of loss.
Whenever the hemoglobin is below normal
A low hemoglobin defines anemia but does not by itself call for parenteral iron. Tell: the trigger is intolerance of or no response to oral iron, not the hemoglobin value.
Intolerance or refractoriness to oral iron
Correct. Parenteral iron is for patients who are intolerant of or refractory to oral iron preparations; it is given over 15 minutes to 1 hour.

set2.q: Which total iron-binding capacity result is expected in iron deficiency anemia?
opts: A normal binding capacity fits anemia of chronic disease (normal or low), not the iron deficiency panel, where it is increased. Tell: iron-poor blood has more free binding sites, so the capacity is high.

Variable describes the red cell distribution width in anemia of chronic disease and the reticulocyte count in iron deficiency, not the binding capacity. Tell: iron deficiency raises the total iron-binding capacity consistently.

Correct. The iron panel of iron deficiency shows a reduced serum ferritin, reduced transferrin saturation and an increased total iron-binding capacity, with microcytic, hypochromic cells. Anemia of chronic disease has the opposite binding capacity, normal or low.

A decreased total iron-binding capacity belongs to anemia of chronic disease, with normal or increased ferritin. Tell: in iron deficiency the binding capacity rises as ferritin falls; in chronic disease both move the other way.

set2.q: Which finding is often the first indication of hemolysis, even before anemia or symptoms appear?
opts: Jaundice is listed among the differentiating features of hemolysis, but often the first indication is a rise in the reticulocyte count, before anemia or symptoms. Tell: the earliest clue can be found on a count before anything shows on the skin.
High-output cardiac failure, chest pain and shock are the severe end of hemolytic anemia, not its first signal. Tell: the first indication can be present without anemia or symptoms at all.

Correct. An unexpected increase in the reticulocyte count, even without anemia or symptoms, should prompt consideration of hemolysis, and it is often the first indication. The marrow is compensating for the shortened red cell life span.

A falling reticulocyte count signals an inadequate bone marrow response, the opposite of hemolysis, which drives a compensatory increase in erythropoiesis. Tell: hemolytic marrow is hyperplastic and pushes reticulocytes up.

set2.q: During an acute attack of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, which peripheral smear findings may be seen?
opts: Sickle-shaped cells are a feature of sickle cell disease, not of an oxidant attack. Tell: the oxidant attack leaves Heinz bodies and a missing chunk, not a sickle shape.

Correct. Without reduced glutathione the red cell is damaged by oxidative stress and Heinz bodies form inside it; splenic macrophages then remove them by taking a chunk out of the cell, leaving bite cells. Both may appear on the smear during an attack.

Ring sideroblasts are not the attack finding; during an attack, a peripheral smear may show Heinz bodies and bite cells. Tell: the oxidant attack forms Heinz bodies, and splenic macrophages take a chunk out of the cell.

Hypersegmented neutrophils are not the attack finding; during an attack, a peripheral smear may show Heinz bodies and bite cells. Tell: this attack damages red cells, so the smear shows red cell changes, Heinz bodies and bite cells.

set2.q: Which test is required to diagnose aplastic anemia?
opts: A peripheral smear is reviewed in the macrocytic workup, but it cannot show stem cell loss in the marrow. Tell: aplastic anemia is a marrow diagnosis, so the marrow must be sampled.

A repeat complete blood count with differential documents pancytopenia and its trend, which is how aplastic anemia is suspected. Tell: the count shows that three cell lines are low; only the marrow biopsy shows why and excludes other causes.
A reticulocyte count shows whether the marrow response is adequate in any anemia, but it is not diagnostic. Tell: the count shows marrow response, not the cause; the bone marrow biopsy is required.

Correct. A bone marrow biopsy is required for the diagnosis of aplastic anemia and to exclude other causes of pancytopenia. Urgent or emergent consultation with a hematologist/oncologist is indicated, and the treatment is bone marrow transplant.

set2.q: After secondary causes are ruled out, what is the initial treatment of autoimmune hemolytic anemia?
opts: Hydroxyurea is not among the treatments listed for autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Tell: autoimmune hemolytic anemia starts with glucocorticoids, then rituximab.

Correct. Treatment of autoimmune hemolytic anemia is glucocorticoids initially, after ruling out secondary causes. Rituximab is the other named agent, with immunosuppressants and splenectomy as further options.
Splenectomy is listed among the other treatment options, behind glucocorticoids and rituximab, not as the first step. Tell: initial therapy is a drug, and surgery waits until it is needed.
Folic acid is part of the supportive treatment of thalassemia; it does nothing to stop antibody-mediated destruction. Tell: an autoimmune process needs suppression, starting with glucocorticoids.

set2.q: Besides cautious transfusion, which supportive measure is part of thalassemia treatment?
opts: Iron overload is already a feature of thalassemia, so adding iron would worsen the problem the treatment list warns about. Tell: the supplement on the list is folic acid.
Glucocorticoids are the initial treatment of autoimmune hemolytic anemia, an antibody disease. Tell: thalassemia is Coombs negative, so there is nothing to suppress; support with folic acid.

Correct. Thalassemia treatment is supportive: transfusion when absolutely necessary (it can exacerbate iron overload), folic acid and genetic counseling. No disease-modifying drug is named for thalassemia.
Hydroxyurea is the disease-modifying drug for sickle cell disease, raising fetal hemoglobin. Tell: the thalassemia list is supportive only, transfusion, folic acid and counseling.

set2.q: Which cause of iron deficiency acts through increased demand rather than loss or poor absorption?
opts: Correct. Increased demand is its own category of iron deficiency: pregnancy and growth in infancy or adolescence. Blood loss, dietary factors and malabsorption are the other categories, so pregnancy is the one that fits demand.

Celiac sprue causes iron deficiency through malabsorption, alongside gastric bypass surgery and food allergies, not through increased demand. Tell: a gut disease that blocks uptake is malabsorption; demand means the body needs more.
Menstrual loss is chronic blood loss, the most common cause of iron deficiency anemia in adults, rather than increased demand. Tell: menses lose iron; pregnancy and growth need more of it.

Heavy tea drinking is listed under dietary factors with a vegan diet and antacids, factors that limit iron intake or uptake, not demand. Tell: a habit that reduces iron coming in is dietary; demand comes from pregnancy or growth.

set2.q: With which condition is acquired sideroblastic anemia usually associated?
opts: Chronic blood loss is not among the listed associations of sideroblastic anemia; the acquired type is usually associated with myelodysplastic syndrome. Tell: hereditary is usually X-linked, acquired usually goes with myelodysplastic syndrome.

Correct. Sideroblastic anemia comes in three types: hereditary (usually X-linked), acquired (usually associated with myelodysplastic syndrome), and acquired reversible, from alcohol, drugs such as isoniazid or chlorambucil, copper deficiency, hypothermia or lead poisoning.
An X-linked defect describes the hereditary type, not the acquired type. Tell: hereditary is X-linked; acquired goes with myelodysplastic syndrome.

Chronic kidney disease is linked to its own anemia and is an indication for erythropoietin, not the usual association of acquired sideroblastic anemia. Tell: the marrow disorder myelodysplastic syndrome is the association.

set2.q: In an elderly patient with a cytopenia, which causes does the lifespan table list to check?
opts: Abnormal newborn screens and inherited anemias are the infant priority. Tell: older adults are checked for iron and B12 deficiency, drugs, kidney disease and marrow disorders.
Pregnancy belongs to the adult row with gastrointestinal or gynecologic blood loss and chronic kidney disease. Tell: the elderly row adds B12 deficiency, drugs and marrow disorders.
Correct. In the elderly, check iron and B12 deficiency, chronic kidney disease, drugs and marrow disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome, and tailor treatment to function, comorbidities and goals.
Heavy menses is the adolescent priority, where counts and ferritin are checked. Tell: the elderly row lists iron and B12 deficiency, kidney disease, drugs and marrow disorders.

set2.q: Which iron panel result shows there is no iron overload?
opts: A saturation above 45 percent fails the rule even with a low ferritin, so overload is not excluded. Tell: the rule needs both values under their cut-offs.
A ferritin above 300 micrograms/L fails the rule even with a low saturation; ferritin also rises as an acute phase reactant. Tell: no overload requires both values below their cut-offs.
Both values above their cut-offs is the pattern that raises concern for overload, the opposite of the reassuring result. Tell: no overload is ferritin under 300 with saturation under 45 percent.

Correct. If ferritin is less than 300 micrograms/L and the transferrin saturation is less than 45 percent, there is no iron overload. Both must be below their cut-offs, and because ferritin is an acute phase reactant the whole laboratory picture is read with caution.

set2.q: What is a defining feature of aplastic anemia?
opts: A low erythropoietin response is the main cause of anemia of chronic kidney disease, which lowers the red cell line. Tell: aplastic anemia drops all three cell lines because the stem cells themselves are gone.

Iron-restricted erythropoiesis, a low transferrin saturation despite normal or high ferritin, occurs in chronic kidney disease. Tell: iron restriction limits red cells only; stem cell loss empties every cell line.

Correct. Loss of hematopoietic stem cells is a defining feature of aplastic anemia, which shows as pancytopenia, loss of red cells, platelets and white cells. Drugs, chemicals, viruses or mutations can alter the stem cells and predispose them to autoimmune destruction.

Impaired deoxyribonucleic acid synthesis defines megaloblastic anemia, with macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Tell: megaloblastic marrow is busy but asynchronous; aplastic marrow has lost its stem cells.

set2.q: Besides hemoglobin and iron, what is monitored in anemia of chronic kidney disease?
opts: Correct. Follow-up of anemia of chronic kidney disease means monitoring hemoglobin, iron and blood pressure, with nephrology for advanced chronic kidney disease, erythropoiesis-stimulating agent decisions or uncertainty. The agent is considered by chronic kidney disease stage, hemoglobin and risk.
Methylmalonic acid separates B12 deficiency from folate deficiency in a macrocytic anemia. Tell: kidney anemia is normocytic and its follow-up list is hemoglobin, iron and blood pressure.
The absolute neutrophil count is followed in leukopenia, where it sets the severity of neutropenia. Tell: kidney anemia follow-up adds blood pressure to hemoglobin and iron.

Haptoglobin falls when free hemoglobin is released in hemolysis, so it monitors red cell destruction. Tell: anemia of chronic kidney disease is a production problem, followed with hemoglobin, iron and blood pressure.

set2.q: Which is a common secondary cause of autoimmune hemolytic anemia?
opts: Correct. Common secondary causes are viruses (human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis, Epstein-Barr virus), autoimmune disorders (lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma, ulcerative colitis), lymphoproliferative disorders such as leukemia, lymphoma and multiple myeloma, and pregnancy.

Oxidative stress, as in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, is a non-antibody cause of hemolysis. Tell: secondary autoimmune causes are viruses, autoimmune disease, lymphoproliferative disease and pregnancy.

Copper poisoning is listed with snake and insect bites and burns as a toxin causing hemolysis. Tell: a toxin damages cells directly, whereas the secondary autoimmune list is diseases that drive antibody production.

Chronic liver disease is listed as a cause of secondary hemochromatosis, the iron overload state. Tell: the lymphoproliferative disorders, not liver disease, are on the secondary autoimmune hemolysis list.

set2.q: When reviewing a new anemia, which value shows whether the bone marrow response is adequate?
opts: Correct. The initial approach reviews the complete blood count across the three cell lines, evaluates for pancytopenia and the mean corpuscular volume, then reviews the reticulocyte index to decide whether the bone marrow response is adequate. Reticulocytes are the newly released red cells, so they measure marrow output.

The mean corpuscular volume is the average red cell size (80-100 fL); it sorts an anemia into small, normal or large cells but says nothing about marrow output. Tell: size classifies the anemia, the reticulocyte index judges the marrow.

The red cell distribution width measures differences in the volume and size of red cells, since healthy cells are about the same size. It describes variation, not marrow production. Tell: width means size spread, not how many new cells are made.

Serum ferritin belongs to the iron panel and reflects iron stores; it is low in iron deficiency and normal or raised in anemia of chronic disease. It does not measure the marrow response. Tell: ferritin is about stores, reticulocytes about output.

set2.q: What is the most frequent cause of B12 deficiency?
opts: Increased demand, as in pregnancy, is a cause of folate deficiency. Tell: the leading cause of B12 deficiency is an autoimmune attack on parietal cells or intrinsic factor, pernicious anemia.

Drugs such as methotrexate, phenytoin and metformin are listed as causes of folate deficiency. Tell: the most frequent cause of B12 deficiency is pernicious anemia, an autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor.

Correct. Pernicious anemia is the most frequent cause of B12 deficiency. It is an autoimmune reaction against parietal cells and/or intrinsic factor itself, so intrinsic factor is not available to carry B12 to the distal ileum, and it brings gastric atrophy and an increased risk of gastric cancer.

Poor diet heads the causes of folate deficiency (impoverished, indigent, alcohol use disorder, elderly), and liver stores of B12 last about 3-4 years. Tell: the most frequent cause of B12 deficiency is autoimmune, pernicious anemia.

set2.q: Why does the distribution of sickle cell disease follow the malaria belt?
opts: Correct. The distribution follows the malaria belt closely because heterozygous carriers of sickle cell trait are 90 percent less likely to experience severe malaria than people with only normal hemoglobin A, a survival advantage where malaria is common.
Malaria does not create the beta globin mutation; it selects for carriers who survive it better. Tell: the advantage is protection from severe malaria in heterozygotes.
This reverses the relationship: heterozygous carriers are 90 percent less likely to have severe malaria. Tell: the trait protects, which is why it persists in malaria regions.
Sickling comes from hemoglobin S polymerizing under low oxygen tension, not from antimalarial drugs. Tell: the map overlap is natural selection, carriers resisting severe malaria.

set2.q: Which oral iron schedule is described as probably best for absorption and side effects?
opts: Taking iron with food reduces side effects but also decreases absorption, so dosing with every meal trades away uptake. Tell: the better idea is less frequent dosing, every other day.
More frequent dosing is the opposite of the finding: less frequent dosing gives better absorption and fewer side effects. Tell: fewer doses absorb better.

Bedtime dosing with milk is not the advice; the alternative preparation is taken in the morning, on an empty stomach with a full glass of orange juice, and alternate-day dosing is the schedule called probably best. Tell: low pH, citric acid and vitamin C help uptake.

Correct. Recent studies show better absorption and fewer side effects with less frequent dosing, and alternate-day dosing is probably best, although adherence can be a problem. Oral iron otherwise has poor absorption, many side effects and poor adherence.

set2.q: What is the leading cause of death for patients with sickle cell disease?
opts: Splenic infarct is one of the tissue infarctions of sickle cell disease, alongside aseptic necrosis of the femoral or humeral heads. Tell: the named leading killer is the lung complication.
Leg ulcers are a chronic manifestation of sickle cell disease, painful but not the leading cause of death. Tell: chest pain, fever, hypoxemia and new infiltrates mark the deadly complication.
Priapism is a listed vaso-occlusive manifestation of sickle cell disease. Tell: the complication with more than 10 percent adult mortality is acute chest syndrome.

Correct. Acute chest syndrome is the leading cause of death in sickle cell disease, often associated with an acute pain event, with greater than 10 percent mortality in adults. Its cause is multifactorial: infection, infarction, pulmonary embolism and fat embolism.

set2.q: If B12 and folate levels are borderline but suspicion continues, which tests come next?
opts: Correct. B12 and folate levels are the initial tests for macrocytic anemia, with a peripheral smear, but they are not very sensitive. If they are borderline or clinical suspicion continues, homocysteine and methylmalonic acid levels are checked: both rise in B12 deficiency, homocysteine alone in folate deficiency.

Ferritin and transferrin saturation belong to the microcytic anemia workup, with serum iron and total iron-binding capacity. Tell: a macrocytic anemia with borderline vitamin levels needs the metabolite tests, not the iron panel.

A bone marrow biopsy is required to diagnose aplastic anemia and exclude other causes of pancytopenia. Tell: borderline B12 or folate is followed by blood metabolite levels, homocysteine and methylmalonic acid, not a marrow biopsy.

Haptoglobin and bilirubin are hemolysis labs, used when red cells are being destroyed. Tell: a megaloblastic picture is a production problem, and borderline vitamin levels are clarified with homocysteine and methylmalonic acid.

set2.q: What should accompany ferrous sulfate because of its most common gastrointestinal side effect?
opts: Antacids (calcium) are listed among the dietary factors that cause iron deficiency, so pairing one with iron works against absorption. Tell: the side effect to plan for is constipation, which a stool softener treats.

Proton pump inhibitors are a medication cause of iron deficiency, so adding one undermines the iron. Tell: the emphasized side effect is constipation, not heartburn, and the partner drug is a stool softener.

Diarrhea is not the emphasized effect; ferrous sulfate causes nausea and especially constipation, so an antidiarrheal would worsen the problem. Tell: constipation is the emphasized side effect, so pair it with a laxative.

Correct. Gastrointestinal side effects of ferrous sulfate are common, nausea and especially constipation, so it is given with at least an as-needed laxative or stool softener. Side effects drive the poor adherence oral iron is known for.

opts: A low ferritin points to depleted stores; in anemia of chronic disease ferritin should be normal or increased, and a value below 30 ng/mL means coexistent iron deficiency. Tell: chronic disease keeps ferritin up.

Correct. Anemia of chronic disease has a ferritin that is normal or increased and a total iron-binding capacity that is decreased (normal or low on the differential), while iron deficiency has a low ferritin and a raised binding capacity. These two values are where the comparisons agree.
A low ferritin with a high total iron-binding capacity is the iron deficiency panel. Tell: in chronic disease the two values flip: ferritin is preserved and binding capacity falls.

opts: High serum iron, saturation and ferritin

Correct. Sideroblastic anemia carries an excess of total body iron, with increased serum iron, transferrin saturation and ferritin. That separates it from iron deficiency, another microcytic anemia in the differential, where all three fall.
A low ferritin with a high total iron-binding capacity is the iron deficiency pattern. Tell: sideroblastic anemia has too much iron, not too little.

Normal or high ferritin with a low total iron-binding capacity is the anemia of chronic disease pattern. Tell: sideroblastic anemia raises serum iron and saturation as well as ferritin.
Low serum iron, saturation and ferritin
All three falling describes depleted iron, the reverse of the excess total body iron in sideroblastic anemia. Tell: in sideroblastic anemia every iron number goes up.

set2.q: An absolute neutrophil count of 1,200 cells per microliter is classified as which degree of neutropenia?
opts: Neutropenia extends up to 1,500 cells per microliter, the top of the mild range, so 1,200 is neutropenic. Tell: anything from 1,000 to 1,500 is mild neutropenia.
Correct. Mild neutropenia is an absolute neutrophil count of 1,000-1,500 cells per microliter, so 1,200 is mild. Moderate is 500-999 and severe is below 500.
Moderate neutropenia is 500-999 cells per microliter, so 1,200 sits above it. Tell: once the count reaches 1,000 the grade is mild.
Severe neutropenia is an absolute neutrophil count below 500 cells per microliter, far below 1,200. Tell: severe is the grade that turns fever into an emergency, and 1,200 is two grades away.
